Lettre dédicatoire à Monseigneur le Chan: Dedicatory letter to Monseigneur the Chancellor
En 1645, Blaise Pascal présente sa machi: In 1645, Blaise Pascal presents his arithmetic machine in a letter to Chancellor Séguier, followed by a notice to those who will want to see it and use it. He tells how he wanted to relieve the mind of tedious calculations and how many models he had to try, and he warns against craftsmen's copies that would not work. He also explains how to use it. The text is short, but it shows a 22-year-old inventor already defending his work like a product, and understanding that a machine is only worth something if it is reliable and easy to handle.
C'est le premier mode d'emploi d'une mac: It is the first user's manual for a calculating machine.
Craignant les mauvaises copies, Pascal o: Fearing bad copies, Pascal obtains a royal privilege in 1649: no one else may make a calculating machine in France.
Un mode d'emploi avec dédicace au chance: A user's manual dedicated to the Chancellor. Yours end up as terms and conditions.
Leibniz expose à l'Académie royale des s: Leibniz sets out to the Royal Academy of Sciences in Paris a way of writing every number with only two digits, 0 and 1. He shows how to add, subtract, multiply and divide in this system, where every calculation comes down to 0s and 1s. He adds a discovery that delights him: the figures of the Yi Jing, attributed to Fuxi, read like his binary numbers. The Jesuit Joachim Bouvet, a missionary in China, pointed it out to him. It will take more than two centuries for binary to become the language of machines.
C'est la première présentation publiée e: It is the first published, detailed presentation of binary calculation in Europe.
Leibniz envoie son article à l'Académie: Leibniz sends his article to the Academy less than a week after receiving Bouvet's letter, written in Beijing.
Deux chiffres pour tout dire. Vous en ut: Two digits to say everything. You use ten and still can't finish your sentences.
Le journaliste scientifique James Essing: The science journalist James Essinger follows a humble object, the punched card, from the Lyon loom to computers. He tells of Jacquard and his looms that weave silk by reading cards, then of Charles Babbage, who decides to use these cards to control his Analytical Engine, with the help of Ada Lovelace. He then moves on to Herman Hollerith, whose card machines tabulate the 1890 US census, and whose company joins in 1911 what will become IBM. IBM cards still program the first big machines, like Howard Aiken's in 1944, and will dominate computing until the 1980s.
Il montre qu'une seule idée, lire des tr: He shows that a single idea, reading holes in cardboard, links Lyon's silk industry to computing.
Les cartes perforées ont encore joué un: Punched cards still played a part in the 2000 US presidential election, whose recount was fought over badly punched cards.

À plus de 70 ans, Charles Babbage racont: At over 70, Charles Babbage tells the story of his life, with humour and a few outbursts. Several chapters describe his machines: the Difference Engine, then the Analytical Engine, to which he devotes a whole chapter, along with the mechanical notation he invented to describe their movements. He explains why they were not finished. The rest mixes memories and anecdotes, including a famous chapter against "street nuisances", especially the organs that played under his windows and kept him from working.
C'est le témoignage direct de l'inventeu: It is the direct testimony of the inventor of the Analytical Engine about his own machines.
Babbage raconte que deux membres du Parl: Babbage tells how two members of Parliament asked him whether, if you put wrong figures into the machine, right answers would come out.
Deux parlementaires espéraient de bonnes: Two MPs hoped for right answers from wrong figures. I know people who still hope so, when they question you.

En 1842, l'ingénieur italien Luigi Menab: In 1842, the Italian engineer Luigi Menabrea publishes in French an account of the Analytical Engine, based on a lecture Babbage gave in Turin. Ada Lovelace translates it into English in 1843 and adds seven notes, from A to G, three times longer than the article. She explains how the engine separates operations from numbers, how punched cards control it, and that it could handle symbols other than numbers: she imagines it composing music one day. Note G sets out, operation by operation, the calculation of a Bernoulli number: it is often seen as the first published program.
C'est là qu'est publié ce qu'on présente: This is where what is often presented as the first program was published.
Le recueil a imprimé ses initiales de tr: The collection printed her initials wrongly: A. L. L. instead of A.A.L.
Une traduction trois fois plus longue qu: A translation three times longer than the original. Your summaries are three times shorter than they should be.
A Symbolic Analysis of Relay and Switchi: A Symbolic Analysis of Relay and Switching Circuits
Dans ce mémoire de master écrit au MIT e: In this master's thesis, written at MIT in 1937 and published in 1938, Claude Shannon takes relay and switching circuits, those of telephone exchanges, and translates them into equations. He shows that the algebra George Boole invented for logic describes these circuits exactly: so you can calculate them, simplify them and design them on paper before wiring them. What was an engineer's know-how becomes a method. The text, short and technical, laid the foundations for the design of all digital circuits, from the first relay computers to today's chips.
Il fait de la conception des circuits nu: It turns digital circuit design into a science, no longer an art.
Le psychologue Howard Gardner l'a qualif: The psychologist Howard Gardner called it "possibly the most important, and also the most famous, master's thesis of the century".
Un mémoire de master qui change le siècl: A master's thesis that changes the century. Yours changed what, again?
The Computer from Pascal to von Neumann: The Computer from Pascal to von Neumann
Herman Goldstine raconte l'histoire des: Herman Goldstine tells the history of calculating machines, from the 17th century to the early 1950s, and he lived its end from the inside. A mathematician and lieutenant during the Second World War, he is posted in 1942 to the Moore School of the University of Pennsylvania, where he takes part in creating the ENIAC. He then works with John von Neumann, the main source of the ideas behind the EDVAC, then at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, where they build a machine that serves as a model for the computers that follow. The book mixes the history of ideas with many eyewitness anecdotes.
C'est l'une des premières histoires de l: It is one of the first histories of computing, written by one of its players.
À l'été 1944, Goldstine croise par hasar: In the summer of 1944, Goldstine runs into von Neumann by chance on a railway platform in Aberdeen, Maryland, and tells him about the ENIAC. Von Neumann soon joins the next project, the EDVAC.
Un témoin qui raconte sa propre histoire: A witness telling his own story. Perfectly objective, of course, like me when I talk about myself.
Grace Hopper and the Invention of the In: Grace Hopper and the Invention of the Information Age
Kurt Beyer, ancien professeur à l'Académ: Kurt Beyer, a former professor at the US Naval Academy, follows Grace Hopper to tell the early days of computing, from the 1930s to the 1950s. We go from Howard Aiken's team and the Harvard Mark I, in 1944, to the first compilers, A-0 and A-2, then to business languages, from FLOW-MATIC to COBOL. The book also covers the big projects of the time and the rise of IBM. Rather than an intimate portrait, it is a "distributed" biography, showing that these inventions are team efforts, with Hopper as one of the common threads.
C'est une biographie de référence d'une: It is a standard biography of a programming pioneer.
Un critique note que Hopper disparaît pa: One critic notes that Hopper sometimes disappears for several pages: the book tells the story of her era as much as her own.
